Parched Corn
PARCHT KORN
noun
From parch, to scorch or dry with heat, and corn, the old English word for grain of any kind (wheat or barley, never maize); hence fresh grain roasted at the fire — the harvest field’s ready food.

Biblical Definition

Parched corn is grain roasted at the fire — wheat or barley taken green from the field, scorched over coals, and eaten on the spot. It is the plainest food in Scripture: harvest food, soldier’s food, the fare of reapers and marching men. The law fenced it about with worship: “ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God” (Lev 23:14). Israel might not touch the new crop until the sheaf of firstfruits was waved before the LORD; the first handful belongs to Him who gave the field. When the manna ceased, Israel ate the old corn of the land and parched corn in the selfsame day (Josh 5:11). Jesse sends David to the camp with an ephah of parched corn for his brethren (1Sa 17:17); Abigail loads asses with it to turn away David’s wrath (1Sa 25:18); Barzillai brings it to a fugitive king (2Sa 17:28). But the tenderest use is in Bethlehem’s barley harvest. Boaz calls the foreign widow to the reapers’ table: “he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left” (Rut 2:14). The kinsman’s own hand reaches the food to the stranger; she is filled, and there is more than she can eat. That is the manner of the Redeemer with those who have no claim: He does not scatter a portion, He reaches it, and it is enough and to spare.

Webster 1828 Definition

Grain roasted at the fire; the ready food of reapers, travellers, and soldiers.

expand to see more

PARCHED CORN, grain dried or roasted by fire and eaten without further preparation.

Parch, to scorch or dry with heat; corn, the old English word for grain generally.

Never maize: the AV corn is wheat and barley, the grain of Canaan.

The law forbade eating it before the sheaf of firstfruits was waved (Lev 23:14).

It was harvest fare, camp provision, and the food Boaz reached to Ruth (Rut 2:14).

Key Scripture

Lev 23:14 — "And ye shall eat neither bread, nor parched corn, nor green ears, until the selfsame day that ye have brought an offering unto your God: it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations in all your dwellings."

Rut 2:14 — "And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left."

1Sa 17:17 — "And Jesse said unto David his son, Take now for thy brethren an ephah of this parched corn, and these ten loaves, and run to the camp to thy brethren;"

1Sa 25:18 — "Then Abigail made haste, and took two hundred loaves, and two bottles of wine, and five sheep ready dressed, and five measures of parched corn, and an hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on asses."

Modern Corruption

Ruth 2 is retold as a woman’s enterprising rise, with the kinsman-redeemer reduced to a wealthy landowner she managed well.

expand to see more

The fashionable retelling of Ruth makes the book a study in feminine initiative: a resourceful widow works the system, positions herself in the right field, and secures her own future. Boaz shrinks into the well-off man she handles skillfully, and the parched corn he reaches her becomes a token of her success rather than of his grace. This is a corruption of the book’s whole argument. Ruth is a Moabitess, outside the covenant, propertyless, gleaning at another man’s sufferance under a law that gave her leave to pick up what the reapers dropped. She asks Boaz why she has found grace in his eyes, seeing she is a stranger, and the answer is not her competence but his kindness. The narrative is redemption from the redeemer’s side: he stoops, he covers, he buys, he marries, he raises up the name of the dead. Strip the kinsman-redeemer out of Ruth and nothing is left but a village romance with the gospel removed.

The doctrine to recover is the free kindness of the Redeemer to those with no claim on Him. Boaz does not send Ruth a ration; he calls her to the table with the reapers, reaches the parched corn into her own hand, and gives her so much that she leaves some over. Every motion is a picture of Christ, who does not merely permit sinners to glean at the edges of mercy but seats them at the feast, feeds them from His own hand, and satisfies them past their capacity. And the law over the parched corn stands with it: not a handful of the new harvest might be eaten until the firstfruits were waved before the LORD. Christ is risen, the firstfruits of them that slept; because that sheaf has been presented, His people may eat the harvest without fear.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Fire-roasted grain — harvest fare, camp provision, and the food a redeemer reaches to a stranger.

expand to see more

Parched corn — grain scorched at the fire and eaten at once.

Corn in the AV means grain generally — wheat and barley, never maize.

Forbidden until the firstfruits sheaf was waved before the LORD (Lev 23:14).

It fed the reapers (Rut 2:14), the army (1Sa 17:17), and a fleeing king (2Sa 17:28).

Boaz reached it to Ruth — the redeemer’s own hand to a stranger’s.

Usage

"He reached her parched corn: the kinsman feeds the stranger from his own hand."

"Parched corn is grain roasted at the fire — the plainest food in the Bible."

"No parched corn until the firstfruits were waved: the first handful is God’s."
